Verdict: ACCEPTThe written arguments justify the tile contraction, the exact interface correction, and the all-width occupied-band uniqueness and inventory. I found no mathematical error requiring revision, and no actual physical capacity is counted twice in the final accounting identity.The essential distinction is handled correctly: the individual  $B_i$  are raw block deficits whose definitions can repeat physical tiles. Their association with distinct blocks does not make them disjoint donor capacities. The exact correction  $X-2J$  removes that repetition, and the note explicitly limits subsequent use to the resulting conservation identity.I use the accepted matching-block independence and two-selection unlocking theorem, together with the prior band feasibility/freezing and positive-graft facts you authorize. I do not use finite validation or Lean execution as evidence for the geometric arguments.There is one evidentiary limit concerning the illustrative graft ledger: without the graft’s coordinates, I can check its arithmetic and its role in the counterexample, but cannot independently reconstruct its individual new ledger integers. The counterexample itself follows from the authorized prior facts and the new nonpositivity lemma, independently of those integers.1. The block–tile connectivity proof is soundConnectivity of the entire endpoint intersectionA nonempty disconnected induced subset of a four-cycle must consist of two opposite corners. If those are the only endpoints in a tile, either remaining corner is adjacent to both endpoints and therefore cannot be selected. Both remaining corners must be blank.Each endpoint then has no occupied neighbor inside the tile and at most two neighbors outside it. This contradicts  $d_A(p)\ge 3$ .Thus  $P\cap Q$  is connected whenever nonempty. One useful consequence, implicit in the note, is that two different connected components of  $G[P]$  cannot share a physical tile. Therefore describing  $\rho$  as the charge summed over whole endpoint components introduces no additional component-level overlap.Connectivity of an individual matching-block intersectionSuppose a block  $C$  meets a tile precisely at opposite corners
$$a=(0,0),\qquad d=(1,1).$$
It cannot be a forced two-vertex block, whose two vertices would be adjacent. It is therefore flexible.Because neither other tile corner belongs to  $C$ , the two allowed neighbors guaranteed at  $a$  must be its two exterior neighbors. The same holds at  $d$ . In particular, all the exterior edges invoked in the proof really are allowed.Now suppose  $b=(0,1)$  is an endpoint outside  $C$ . In any perfect matching its mate cannot be  $a$  or  $d$ , since a matching edge is allowed and would join their blocks. Its mate is therefore either  $(-1,1)$  or  $(0,2)$ .If its mate is  $(-1,1)$ , combine that matching restriction with a matching of  $C$  containing  $a(-1,0)$ . The two matched edges are opposite sides of the square with corners
$$(0,0),(0,1),(-1,1),(-1,0).$$
Flipping this square produces a perfect matching containing  $ab$ , contradicting the distinction between their blocks.If its mate is  $(0,2)$ , use a matching of  $C$  containing  $d(1,2)$ . The square flip now produces the edge  $bd$ , giving the same contradiction.This is a valid application of the accepted independence theorem. Only one prescribed edge within  $C$  is chosen in each case. The other prescribed edge belongs to a distinct block. There is no assumption that two arbitrary allowed edges within one block can occur simultaneously.The reflected argument excludes  $c=(1,0)$  as an endpoint. Neither  $b$  nor  $c$  can be selected, because each is adjacent to both  $a$  and  $d$ . Both are blank, again contradicting  $d_A(a)\ge3$ .Boundary sites cause no exception: if one of the required exterior neighbors is missing, the assertion that the flexible endpoint has two allowed neighbors already fails.This establishes the geometry needed for contraction. No intersection-splitting correction has been omitted.2. The raw block nonpositivity proof uses the actual supports correctlyThe accepted two-selection theorem is applied in the original full endpoint graph, with its actual selection set  $T$ . Its hypotheses match:the original pair is feasible;every endpoint has occupied degree at least three;the endpoint in question belongs to a flexible allowed-edge block;exchange terminality excludes the replacement matching and feasible promotion bundle supplied by the theorem.There is no need to assume that a block considered in isolation retains the original degree condition. In particular, endpoints of other blocks remain occupied endpoints throughout the argument.For a flexible block, the local contribution is
$$\frac n2+t_Q-2,\qquad n=|C_i\cap Q|.$$
The bounds are: $n$ Bound on  $t_Q$ Upper bound on the local contribution $1$  $t_Q\le1$  $-\tfrac12$  $2$  $t_Q\le1$  $0$  $3$  $t_Q=0$  $-\tfrac12$  $4$  $t_Q=0$  $0$ The only less immediate entry is  $n=1$ . Among the other three corners, any adjacent selected pair contains a vertex adjacent both to its selected partner and to the endpoint, violating feasibility. Thus the only possible two-selection arrangement consists of the two corners adjacent to the endpoint. That gives the flexible endpoint two selected neighbors, which exchange terminality excludes through the accepted theorem.For  $n=2$ , adjacent endpoints leave two adjacent corners that cannot both be selected. Diagonal endpoints would prohibit either remaining corner from being selected; although Section 2 has already excluded that block intersection, including it in the local inequality does no harm. For  $n=3$ , the remaining corner touches two endpoints.Consequently every flexible block has  $\gamma_i\le0$ , tile by tile.Forced blocksFor a forced pair lying within one tile, the two remaining corners cannot both be selected: they are adjacent and each already touches an endpoint. Hence
$$\gamma_i=1+t_Q-2\le0.$$
For a pair crossing two tiles, the three displayed pairs partition all six other sites. Each pair consists of adjacent vertices, with at least one already adjacent to  $p$  or  $q$ . Selecting both members would give that selected vertex at least two occupied neighbors. Thus
$$t_{\mathrm{left}}+t_{\mathrm{right}}\le3,$$
and
$$\gamma_i=1+t_{\mathrm{left}}+t_{\mathrm{right}}-4\le0.$$
This proof needs only feasibility. Extra endpoints or selections outside the two tiles cannot invalidate the upper bound.The warning about tilewise forced-block charges is necessary and correct. A forced endpoint alone in a tile with two selections contributes  $+\tfrac12$ , even though its entire block has nonpositive charge.The positive whole-tile classification is also correct. The only positive possibility is
$$|P\cap Q|=1,\qquad t_Q=2,$$
with whole-tile charge  $+\tfrac12$ . Under exchange terminality, that endpoint must belong to a forced block. This identifies the location of positive tiles without assigning compensation.3. The interface count and the  $2J$  correction are exactThe contraction can be verified directly by counting internal edges, avoiding any ambiguity about cycles or loops in a quotient.Write  $n_Q=|P\cap Q|$ .If  $P\cap Q$  is a proper nonempty subset of the tile, it is a tree. Every block intersection is connected, so the number of edges internal to those intersections is
$$\sum_{i:C_i\cap Q\ne\varnothing}\bigl(|C_i\cap Q|-1\bigr)
=n_Q-m_Q.$$
The endpoint intersection has  $n_Q-1$  edges in total. Hence
$$e_Q=(n_Q-1)-(n_Q-m_Q)=m_Q-1.$$
If the tile is full and mixed, every block intersection is a proper connected subset of the square and is therefore a tree. There are  $4-m_Q$  internal edges among the four square edges, giving
$$e_Q=4-(4-m_Q)=m_Q.$$
This calculation retains parallel interface edges automatically.If all four endpoints belong to one block, then  $m_Q=1$  and  $e_Q=0$ . Its internal square cycle supplies no interface correction.Thus, with  $j_Q$  the indicator of a mixed full tile,
$$e_Q=m_Q-1+j_Q.$$
A mixed full tile has  $t_Q=0$ , so
$$(2-t_Q)e_Q=(2-t_Q)(m_Q-1)+2j_Q.$$
Summing gives precisely
$$X-2J=\sum_{Q\in R}(m_Q-1)(2-t_Q).$$
The weight is therefore exactly  $2-t_Q$ , and the full-square correction is exactly two per mixed full tile.The repeated raw receiver terms cancelExpanding the definitions,
$$\sum_i\gamma_i
=\frac{|P|}{2}+\sum_{Q\in R}m_Q(t_Q-2),$$
whereas
$$\rho=\frac{|P|}{2}+\sum_{Q\in R}(t_Q-2).$$
Their difference is
$$\rho-\sum_i\gamma_i
=\sum_{Q\in R}(m_Q-1)(2-t_Q)
=X-2J.$$
This proves the ledger identity without an allocation assumption.The strongest direct check against double counting is local. Put
$$d_Q=2-t_Q,
\qquad
b_Q=m_Qd_Q-\frac{n_Q}{2}.$$
Here  $b_Q$  is the algebraic contribution to  $B$  from a tile; it need not be nonnegative individually. Then
$$\begin{aligned}
b_Q+2j_Q-d_Qe_Q
&=m_Qd_Q-\frac{n_Q}{2}+2j_Q
-d_Q(m_Q-1+j_Q)\\
&=d_Q-\frac{n_Q}{2}+t_Qj_Q\\
&=2-t_Q-\frac{n_Q}{2},
\end{aligned}$$
because  $t_Qj_Q=0$ .The last expression is exactly that physical tile’s deficit, counted once.For example, a mixed full tile meeting  $m_Q$  blocks contributes
$$(2m_Q-2)+2-2m_Q=0,$$
as it must: four endpoints and no selections exactly use its half-area allowance. The positive-looking  $2J$  term is a correction to the interface count, not a new donor.Endpoint-free tiles contribute  $D$ , also once each. Therefore
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
=D+B+2J-X$$
is a genuine physical accounting identity.Scope of the sufficient classesThe stated sufficient condition gives
$$X\le D+2J
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|\ge B\ge0.$$
If every endpoint tile meets one block, then  $X=J=0$ , and the exact margin is  $D+B$ .These conclusions apply to the stated exchange-terminal class satisfying the degree hypothesis and the respective additional physical condition. They establish no unrestricted compensation theorem.The unrestricted missing inequality is indeed exactly
$$X\le D+B+2J.$$
Through the ledger, it is equivalent to the desired half-area bound; the note does not claim to have proved it.4. The omitted-interface-tax counterexample is validUsing the authorized prior graft facts, the receiver is exchange-terminal and has
$$\rho=1.$$
Section 3 gives nonpositive raw charges for its matching blocks. Those facts alone disprove the inference
$$\bigl(\forall i,\ \gamma_i\le0\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\rho\le0.$$
In particular, neither the exact two-matching count nor the new numerical ledger is needed to establish that obstruction.The displayed numerical ledger is consistent:

X-2J=22.$$

$$\sum_i\gamma_i=-21,\qquad X=28,\qquad J=3,
\qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{flexible}}=-5$$
cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text alone without the graft coordinates or a tile inventory. I regard them as the illustrative reconstructed data described in your prompt, not as independently derived quantities in this review. This limitation does not affect the general ledger or the counterexample’s existence. Even without those values, the ledger proves

for the stipulated receiver.The note also correctly distinguishes this from a counterexample to the global bound. On the stated board, the total margin is
